Example: There is strong evidence that extreme weather is increasing in the UK. The Cockermouth flood of 2009 saw record rainfall of 314 mm in 24 hours, and cost £275 million in insurance claims. Record temperatures have been set in recent years, and winter rainfall has increased. Climate change is driving these trends — warmer oceans increase evaporation, leading to heavier rainfall, while rising temperatures increase the risk of heatwaves and drought. However, the UK is an HIC with resources to respond. The £4.5 million flood defence scheme in Cockermouth (flood walls, embankments, dredging) has reduced future risk. The Environment Agency now uses social media for real-time flood warnings. While events may be more frequent, the UK’s ability to prepare and respond means damage can be managed. On balance, frequency is increasing due to climate change, but the UK’s wealth allows it to invest in defences that limit the damage.

Example: The tropical rainforest is arguably the most important biome because it contains between 50% and 90% of all species on Earth, despite covering only 6% of the land surface. Rainforests have been called the ‘lungs of the world’ as they produce about 20% of the world’s oxygen. They are also a source of medicines — 25% of modern drugs originate from rainforest plants. The rapid nutrient cycle and layered structure create habitats for millions of species. However, other biomes are also vital — oceans absorb more CO₂ than rainforests and produce more oxygen. Polar ice caps regulate global temperatures. Grasslands and farmlands feed the world’s population. Overall, while the TRF is extremely important for biodiversity, climate regulation and medicine, it is one part of a global system where all biomes play essential roles.
